review_title: My Experience With WirelessSource and The Reputation MD
review_comment: The product arrived damaged and not in the advertised 'excellent' condition. There were many dents along the bottom, and the battery health was 71% instead of the advertised 80%. There may be a message under this review stating that 'the fulfillment issues associated with this order were not due to the seller.' If such a message is present, it is incorrect. The problems were not due to the shipping company or Amazon, they were entirely due to the actions of the seller, Wireless Source, and the review management company they contracted, The Reputation MD. I bought a 256GB Apple iPhone 13 from WirelessSource, also known as Magnakom. This review will detail my experience with this seller. To remain objective, I will describe exactly what happened. When the iPhone arrived, I immediately noticed several bumps and dents on its bottom edge. While concerning, I was willing to overlook it so long as the battery health was above 80%. The iPhone was stated to be in excellent condition on its Amazon listing, and, among other things, the battery health was 71% instead of 80%, meaning the iPhone was not in excellent condition. I figured that WirelessSource would rather keep some of the money than refund me all of it, so I sent a message offering to keep the phone if they would refund me the cost of a new battery. WirelessSource replied by sending a generic message offering a 5% refund if I were to keep the phone, and asked for photos of the problem despite me having already sent them. I let them know I had already sent them, and they sent me a variation of the same message, again asking for pictures. Seeing this and doing additional research on WirelessSource, I made a complaint through the Better Business Bureau. WirelessSource then asked for the IMEI of the device, which I provided. They then claimed it wasn't the same as the IMEI of the phone they shipped. When I pushed back and opted to return the phone instead, they asked for a photo of the packaging, and when I provided it, they conceded that it was the phone they sent, and provided me a shipping label to return it. It was around this time that I began receiving calls and emails from a Todd Lewis of The Reputation MD, a company that regulates and 'cleans up' online reviews for businesses. I ignored these, because I thought speaking to a review management company was abnormal. Returning things at Target, Walmart, eBay, or Amazon itself never required me to do that. Also during this time, WirelessSource sent me a message claiming my device was iCloud locked: i.e. I didn't wipe the iPhone before returning it. I did wipe the iPhone, and after a few back-and-forth messages and photos, (including one where they claimed the IMEI didn't match the order even though we previously confirmed it did,) I recorded a video of me going to my Apple account and FindMyiPhone and demonstrating that I had wiped the phone and it was no longer on my account. After that video, they confirmed the account removal. While this was happening, I filed an A-z Refund claim with Amazon. I didn't have a whole lot of faith that I would be refunded at this point. While the claim was active, Todd Lewis of The Reputation MD sent me a 'refund contract.' This contract was meant to ensure I returned the iPhone (even though at that point they had already received it back,) and it was also meant to prevent me from defaming the company, although I suspected they would try and leverage the contract to prevent me from leaving a negative review. I am not making a concrete claim, though, it was just a suspicion I had. Like before, no other refund I've done has made me do this, and I ignored the contract despite their daily emails. Eventually, Amazon themselves refunded me, and I chose to let the Better Business Bureau complaint go. I continued to ignore their emails, since attempting to get a refund from them on top of Amazon's would be fraud, and eventually they stopped. I wanted to leave this review to recount my experience with WirelessSource/Magnakom as well as Todd Lewis and The Reputation MD. I've tried to be objective so you can draw your own conclusions. I have provided a compilation of the messages between us, although it may take some zooming to see them all. I hope you find this review helpful, and I hope WirelessSource learns to do better.

review_title: Proceed With Caution Before Buying Renewed Premium
review_comment: In a nutshell: only buy an Amazon Renewed Premium phone if you are very confident you will keep it. If there is a problem or you decide to return it, the return process can be far more difficult and time-consuming than many buyers would expect. In my case, resolving the return and refund took over twenty-nine calls and nine hours of time. As for the phone itself, “salvage” felt closer than “premium” for the condition of the one I received. The battery health was at 100%, which I appreciated. The packaging was an Amazon Renewed box, which was adequate but not especially reassuring for a phone in this price range. The plastic film on the phone was poorly fitted and added to the impression that this was not a carefully packaged premium product. When I first accessed iOS, I was prompted to “Finish Repairing Your Back Glass,” which indicated that the phone had previously been damaged and repaired. I assume the damage had been fully repaired before resale, and the phone may function perfectly well for some buyers, but this is worth knowing in advance. My concern was that I had no way of knowing where the repairs had been done or to what standard. I also found that Apple warranty coverage did not appear to be active when I checked, despite the phone being less than a year old at the time of purchase. That may not matter to every buyer, but it was one more reason this did not feel comparable to an Apple-refurbished device. I ultimately decided to return it because of the Max size. I ordered it for the added battery life, but once I had it in hand, I realized it was too large for most of my pockets, making it impractical. Since I had only used it for about 10 to 15 minutes, I factory reset it and packed it back up immediately. The return process was the most frustrating part of the experience. Amazon only gave me one return option: UPS pickup. I was not given any practical control over that process. There was no pickup window, and not even a specific day was given. I only realized pickup attempts had begun after finding UPS “sorry we missed you” notices. I work from home, but on a farm, and I am not always near the front of the property. Even though my phone number was available and posted clearly at the entrance, I was never contacted to coordinate the pickup. This created an obvious problem: I was uncomfortable leaving a package worth over $1,000 unattended near the road, but I also was not given a straightforward alternative. I asked whether I could simply take the package to a UPS Store myself, but that was not initially offered as an option. I spent a significant amount of time on the phone with both Amazon and UPS trying to resolve the issue. Eventually I was able to get the return label and complete the return, but only after multiple calls and far more effort than should have been necessary. For an item at this price point, I found the return process unreasonably cumbersome. So my final view is this: the phone may be acceptable for some buyers, especially if they are certain they want to keep it and are comfortable with the realities of the renewed market. But my experience did not match what I expected from something labeled “Renewed Premium,” and the return process was difficult enough that I would urge buyers to proceed with caution.

review_title: Für 120 € ein wirklich super Kauf – perfekt für die OmaFür 120 € ein wirklich super Kauf – perfekt für die Oma
review_comment: Ich habe das iPhone SE der 3. Generation mit 64 GB in Mitternacht im Jahr 2026 als generalüberholtes Gerät für meine Oma gekauft und bin wirklich positiv überrascht. Gerade für 120 € bekommt man hier meiner Meinung nach noch erstaunlich viel Smartphone fürs Geld. Das Gerät ist natürlich nicht mehr das neueste iPhone, aber für den vorgesehenen Zweck absolut ausreichend und auch 2026 noch problemlos brauchbar. Für jemanden, der hauptsächlich telefoniert, Nachrichten schreibt, Fotos macht, WhatsApp nutzt und gelegentlich im Internet unterwegs ist, reicht die Leistung vollkommen aus. Durch die kompakte Größe und den Home-Button ist es außerdem gerade für ältere Menschen angenehm und unkompliziert zu bedienen. Der Zustand des generalüberholten Geräts ist ebenfalls sehr gut. Das Gehäuse sieht wirklich sehr ordentlich aus und weist kaum sichtbare Gebrauchsspuren auf. Am Display sind zwar ein paar kleinere Kratzer vorhanden, diese sind aber im Alltag überhaupt nicht störend und fallen bei eingeschaltetem Display praktisch nicht auf. Insgesamt macht das iPhone einen deutlich besseren Eindruck, als ich es bei einem generalüberholten Gerät in dieser Preisklasse erwartet hätte. Auch der Akku hat noch 91 % Restkapazität, was für ein gebrauchtes bzw. generalüberholtes Gerät absolut in Ordnung ist. Für die Nutzung meiner Oma reicht die Akkuleistung problemlos aus und ich sehe bei diesem Wert keinen Grund, den Akku direkt tauschen zu lassen. Die Einrichtung war wie bei einem iPhone gewohnt unkompliziert und auch die Performance ist für den Alltag noch völlig ausreichend. Besonders positiv finde ich, dass man für relativ wenig Geld ein richtiges iPhone mit Touch ID, guter Kamera, kompakter Bauweise und weiterhin brauchbarer Leistung bekommt. Fazit: Wer 2026 ein günstiges, kleines und zuverlässiges Smartphone für einen eher normalen Alltagsgebrauch sucht, macht mit dem iPhone SE 3. Generation meiner Meinung nach noch immer einen guten Kauf. Für 120 € war es für meine Oma jedenfalls eine hervorragende Wahl. Der sehr gute optische Zustand und die 91 % Akkukapazität haben den positiven Eindruck noch einmal bestätigt. Von mir daher ganz klar 5 Sterne.

Considering an Apple Certified Refurb of same model and storage would be close to $1000, this was a very good value. My thinking was the battery state was probably the vulnerable aspect. So, even if I had to replace the battery after the 90 day warranty, the $100 cost was still be a financial win. (Hopefully, the battery lives as long as my iPhone XR did, haha). I rate the product and experience 4.75 - 5 stars, with a very high level recommendation.

review_title: If at first you get a defective phone, try again if you have the patience.
review_comment: My phone rated Excellent Premium was defective in a way any technician would have identified had it really been tested and reviewed before publishing the phone on Amazon's website. Amazon give the impression that the customer should feel some comfort because of it's rating and because they are Amazon. That doesn't work that way. When you contact Amazon they ask about the problem and then pass on to the seller a very abridged summary. They assure you they will help. But all the conversation between you and Amazon disappears. If you want to preserve this conversation and refer back, or follow up, it is nowhere to be found. They claim to have a buyer/seller message board, but Amazon is invisible and you can't ask for more help. It turns out that part of my biggest problem was how to discover why the phone did not work. I didn't know that an Excellent premium phone can be tested and verified without the updated IOS version being downloaded and installed, and it can't. But no where are you told that. I spent hours on the phone with the carrier and texting with AI because I couldn't even get Apple to acknowledge my Apple account. Then after all my efforts I was locked out for 2 hours! It seems to me this is vital info for a new buyer like me, and it should be included by Amazon in their description. As it turned out the "board" connecting the eSim that issues the signal for cellular to work was defective. But no experts that I consulted realized that a simple test of the eSim is to try to read a Qr code, without a functioning eSim that will not be possible and certainly that is a simple test for verifying a several hundred dollar phone before giving it an Excellent premium rating in Amazon. For several other reasons too lengthy for this review, I now believe Amazon's rating of refurbished phones is BS. And their help is minuscule. Despite that, I ordered a replacement iPhone 15 pro through Amazon, again got suckered in on a non updated IOS, but so far, now that my Apple a/c is recognized, the phone appears to be truly excellent. I knew enough to avoid the extra cost of PREMIUM. Update, I'm still waiting for my refund on the first phone 19 days after paying for it. I've updated my review from one to 3 stars because the replacement phone is in excellent condition as rated, and much more deserving of a Premium designation, which the seller did not claim. I remain disappointed in the Amazon role in the transaction but they do have a large inventory to choose from. Why can't Amazon include in it's sale promotion description a warning to be sure to check whether the phone has the latest IOS upgrade, don't trust the seller. Not knowing to do this cost meat at least half a day all told.

review_comment: Aside from the phone being nearly perfect, no visible signs of wear and tear, no delays (after updating and restoring), unlocked, and the battery is good (84% health). (lengthy story and complaint incoming) However, (and hopefully this helps someone else who faces the same problem) I’m giving it 3 stars because I had the worse experience setting it up. Not to mention the charging cable that came with it didn’t work. Anyway, to the pressing issue here I did what I would normally do when setting up a new iPhone and followed the prompts to transfer my data through the cloud onto this device. However, due to the phone’s software being completely outdated (ios18, we’re on 26) it caused the phone to completely glitch out midway and got extremely hot. I couldn’t swipe up to input my passcode to proceed with the installation process. Heck, I couldn’t even force restart it. (quickly press the volume up, volume down immediately after and press and hold the power button until you see the Apple logo) I was almost at my wits end. Fast forward, the device is still glitchy so I reached out to Amazon Customer Care and was advised that I should take it into Apple and if they couldn’t do anything then to proceed with returning it. I obviously didn’t wanna do that. So I attempted to research the issues and after being pulled between Apple’s forum and Reddit’s forum, I decided to put the iPhone in DFU mode. This mode allows you to update and restore the phone via a computer. So boom, it’s in DFU mode and i’m still struggling! So I contact Apple but of course before doing so I see if they’re able to replace a software defective device out of warranty and of course it was a hard no. At this point, I’m ready to give up and just return it but after letting it die out (due to overheating) I let it charge overnight and said “let’s give this oneee more try.” So, I plugged it back into my computer.. same issue. It would pretend to restore and update the device but I would get an error message midway and couldn’t get my phone out of DFU. Only way to get it out was by completing the restoration. Anyway, I looked up the error message it mentioned that it could be a software issue (tell me something i don’t know 🤷🏽‍♀️) or it could be a charger cable issue.. Hmm 🤔 So I switched charging cables (even bought a new one that I would later use) and low and behold the update and restoration finally WORKED… So all in all, I say all of that to say; if you’re having issues with accessing and fully using your new iPhone. It’s more than likely because its software is extremely outdated. What worked for me: Put your phone in DFU mode (look it up if unsure how). Download either Apple Devices (Windows) or iTunes (Mac). While in DFU mode, plug the device up using a USB to lightning Apple Certified cable. A prompt will display saying error something would you like to proceed with restoring or updating? Click “restore” and then “update and restore” (for some reason it didn’t work clicking update first) it’ll take some time but after that it should go through the process of updating and restoring back to the factory settings and then you can proceed with setting the iPhone up as normal. (important!!! the cable needs to be APPLE CERTIFIED not the one from sheetz up the street) I haven’t experienced any delays or issues since updating to the latest version of iOS but i’m giving 3 stars because 1.) the charger it came with didn’t work. and 2.) because i feel like a little help card should’ve been included considering it didn’t have the latest version of iOS on there. Hopefully, TalkTek takes this review into consideration to include a little note in the packaging on updating the device.

review_comment: Today is Wednesday, August 20, 2025. I’ve always wanted the iPhone 13 Pro Max in Alpine Green ever since it was released, so I decided to give this seller a chance despite the mixed reviews and their 4.5-star rating. I ordered the iPhone 13 Pro Max, Alpine Green, 256GB – Unlocked, Renewed (Excellent Condition). Unfortunately, my experience was disappointing. First, the phone arrived a day late, even though I’m a Prime member (not necessarily the seller’s fault, but still frustrating). When I finally opened the package, the phone was the wrong color (Silver instead of Alpine Green) and had noticeable scratches and chips around the camera lens and aluminum frame. While some wear is expected on a refurbished phone, this was advertised as “Excellent Condition,” and I expected better. To be fair, I still tested the phone. I went into the settings to check everything: Verified the IMEI and serial number to ensure the device was legitimate. Confirmed it was fully unlocked with no SIM restrictions. Checked for any non-Apple parts — thankfully, everything appeared original. The phone’s functions worked well (Face ID, speakers, cameras, flash, vibration, etc.). The screen looked great with almost no scratches, the phone screen sensitivity could have been more proactive, and the back glass was in good condition. However, the biggest disappointment was the battery health: only 77%. According to Amazon’s “Renewed Excellent” standards, it should be at least 80%. For the price I paid, this was unacceptable. As a busy college student, I don’t have the time to send the phone back, but I do feel let down. I’ll likely have to spend another ~$100 to replace the battery at my university’s tech repair shop. Overall, I’m leaving 4 stars because the phone does function well and matches the storage capacity I ordered, but the wrong color, poor battery health, and condition not matching the description made this purchase very frustrating. My advice: check the IMEI, serial, SIM restrictions, and battery health right away when buying renewed iPhones, and read the reviews carefully before purchasing. P.S. I purchased a screen protector separately for extra protection. Also, note that the box only included a USB Lightning cable — no charging adapter. If you don’t already have one, I recommend buying an adapter or a complete charger along with the phone.

review_comment: Aside from a few nitpicks which I'll refer to in this post, the phone I received is pretty much exactly as is detailed in the product description. Face ID works as expected, and out of the box it has a battery health of 86% (not at all perfect, but for a refurbished phone it's pretty good!), which is essentially as described by seller. Both the front and rear cameras work as expected, and so far produce images and videos just as well as if it were bought new from Apple. As expected, the device came with a charger, though keep in mind that (in line with all Apple products nowadays) these are now often sold as USB-C to Lightning cables, as opposed to USB 3.0. For that reason, make sure you have a port/adapter which takes USB-C cables, or have an existing lightning cable you can use. I'm also pleasantly surprised at how visibly clean the phone is - after reading a few reviews on this page for the "excellent quality" version of this refurb, I was expecting to see a few imperfections. Thankfully though, I seem to have gotten lucky. After a few minutes of looking over it, I can't spot a single hairline crack or any points of damage on the edge/back of the phone. Regardless I'd advise caution if this is a concern you have when purchasing, as this has been an uncommon yet known problem with this seller. The only noteworthy issue I have with the product is I sadly didn't receive a pin to open the SIM tray - thankfully I do keep some spare around my house, but had I not, this would've been a pain to sort out. Just in case, I would recommend making sure you have a SIM tray pin/alternative thin metal item, on the off-chance they don't remember to put one in the box for you. As a side point, it's important to be aware that non-Apple approved refurbishment businesses often do not necessarily use OEM (original equipment manufacturer) parts. While this is noted in this product's description, do keep it in mind. This is *very* rarely a problem as non-OEM parts - in my experience - work just as good as original, but they have been known to cause dilemmas. Things like weaker screen glass, less water resistance, and weaker battery overall. Regardless, if you're buying refurbished these can usually be ignored for the lower price. In conclusion, I'd personally recommend this if you're looking for a cheaper device but still want an iPhone/iOS device. Whether it be for the icloud, Apple's ecosystem, or purely for the feel/user experience, it does its job, and does it well. I hope this review helped you come to a decision on your purchase, whether you bought it or not :).

review_comment: I purchased an Amazon Renewed iPhone 14 Pro Max (128GB, Deep Purple) in Excellent condition because I was willing to pay extra for a device that was supposed to be thoroughly inspected and fully functional. Unfortunately, the phone I received was nowhere near "Excellent." The biggest issue is the camera system. One of the main reasons I chose the iPhone 14 Pro Max was for its three-camera setup. However, only one camera works properly in Photo mode. In Video mode, two cameras work, while the third doesn't work at all. The 0.5x ultra-wide camera is completely unavailable, and the 5x zoom function doesn't work either. This is especially frustrating because I'm an up-and-coming mechanic, and I regularly use the 0.5x camera to take photos in tight spaces while working on customers' vehicles. It's an important tool for my job, not just a feature I wanted. I upgraded from an iPhone 13 Pro Max where two of the cameras had failed, so I was excited to finally have a phone with all three cameras working. Instead, I ended up with another phone that has camera issues. At that point, I could have saved money by buying an iPhone 14 Plus with only two cameras and probably received a phone that actually worked. Another concern was that the phone was not properly factory reset. The packaging states that Amazon Renewed devices are supposed to be factory reset before being resold. However, when I powered it on, it started up like a normal phone instead of taking me through the initial setup process. It appeared the previous owner had simply signed out of their Apple ID rather than the phone being completely erased and reset. I contacted Amazon Customer Support to request a replacement since the phone was defective. I was told there were no more iPhone 14 Pro Max devices in Excellent condition available to send as a replacement. However, when I checked the same Amazon listing, it still showed the exact same phone in Excellent condition available for purchase. I don't understand why replacements weren't available when the listing indicated more were in stock. I would have been happy to return the defective phone in exchange for a properly functioning one. I understand that Amazon Renewed products are used, and I wasn't expecting a brand-new phone. However, I did expect to receive the condition I paid for and a device with all advertised features working correctly. A phone with a partially functioning camera system should never pass inspection as "Excellent," especially when customers are paying a premium for that condition. Overall, this experience was extremely disappointing. Amazon Renewed is supposed to give customers confidence that devices have been inspected and tested. Based on my experience, the inspection process failed, and customer service did not provide a reasonable solution.

review_title: Renewed is an excellent alternative, and this watch is incredible
review_comment: I purchased from seller YY wireless. I was worried about purchasing a renewed product but it showed up quickly, came in original box with all original paperwork and OEM charger. Physical condition is perfect, all buttons and bezel work perfectly. No scratches on screen and battery is great. Aside from the seller, the watch 8 classic is amazing. I started with the 4 but when the rotating bezel came out on watch 6 classic I immediately upgraded. I ended up losing that watch when I moved which was completely my fault, and I was really bummed. As soon as I was financially able I wanted the 8. I love it. As a woman with smaller wrists the 46mm is kinda of big but not overly huge. The hybrid leather strap is the way to go. The rotating bezel just looks so classy. With the new update we can now do blood pressure as well as ekg and blood oxygen levels. When I had the watch 4 the ekg tracker was the only way I was able to get a doctor to listen that I was experiencing arrhythmia and was diagnosed with myocarditis earlier than I would have been otherwise. Its life saving. The step counter seems to be extremely accurate as well as heart rate. I love that I can set the fitness mode to log which activity I was doing. Samsung Health and Google Health both are compatible and are exceptional. I have the samsung galaxy s26 ultra and the buds 4 pro and have had flawless connectivity with both. I love that I can control the camera with the watch so if I have it set on a tripod using the back camera I can use the watch as a viewfinder. I can control the buds 4 pro playback and ambient/active noise canceling from my watch. Along with everything else a smart watch does, these things are just so convenient to have.

review_title: Awesome, awesome iPhone.  I'm in love again.
review_comment: I purchased a renewd iPhone Air and saved $147 over new. The only difference between mine and new was that mine had been charged to 100%, 15 times. What's that, two weeks of use before someone returned it? The condition was flawless and I have a one year warranty provided with the purchase. My thoughts: CAMERA The majority of happy, giddy, ecstatic iPhone Air owners are not content creators and think the iPhone Air is awesome. YouTube reviewers depend on their mobile phones to produce video and photos and are not the best judge of the iPhone Air that isn't the very best at producing media. I am not a content creator, but was a professional photographer many years and I am extremely happy with the photos the Air produces. I am retired now and no longer need to shoot in RAW for extensive editing. My previous iPhone 15 Pro took very good photos, but I had to spend time editing in order to back off of the extreme automated processing of the phone's software algorithims. I shot photos at a birthday party at night, outdoors, only lit by string lighting and found the photos to be very natural, not overly processed, well exposed with an absence of grain, even cropping in 3-5x. AUDIO Yes, the Air does not play with stereo speakers. But it is very loud and clear and basically when not using my airpods or using airplay to a bluetooth speaker, it is just fine, no issues. Think about it, how often do you depend on your phone to play loud stereo music? You can always stream to a bluetooth stereo speaker or home stereo or wear your airpods. BATTERY I do a lot of streaming music and podcasts during the day 2-4 hrs worth, receive/answer emails, a lot of texts and take photos and send via iMessage and I'm finding my battery still has 30-50% battery left at 6pm. I don't typically put my phone on a charger during the day and by 6pm I'm ready to eat dinner and relax in the evening so sitting my phone on a magsafe charger stand is an easy way to finish out the day. I did buy Anker's Magsafe power bank that matches the iPhone Air (white) but I've not used it much, more out of convenience because I had it rather than as a necessity. So far I am pleased with the battery performance. It's 3pm right now and the phone has been off of the charger since 7am and there is still 84% battery, without much use though, but that is impressive. DESIGN, WEIGHT, FUNCTION I am enjoying the thinness of the Air, easy to hold, slides into my pocket and the screen is brilliant and easy to see, even in sunshine. I am coming from an iPhone 15 Pro, so the screen is much bigger than I'm used to but it's nice. The processor is very fast and 120Hz pro-motion is extremely nice. WRAP-UP What are the downsides? Without a case, it is very slippery and for that reason alone I ended up buying an extremely thin Aramid case from Pitaka to increase the grip. I wasn't worried too much about scratches as I am very careful with my phones, but now I admit, I can relax alittle and I believe the case actually improved the look of the AIR rather than detracted. There wasn't a reason to upload a phone of the phone, you can see those everywhere.

review_comment: I wanted to love this thing. A renewed iPhone 16e at a discount felt like a smart move, modern iOS, A18 chip, USB-C, IP68, the whole package. I talked myself into it. Then I actually used it. The performance is genuinely good. The A18 is fast, apps snap open, and Apple Intelligence works as advertised. Battery life impressed me more than I expected, easily a full day and then some with room to spare. The 6.1-inch OLED display looks great indoors. The camera is where things got real. One lens. Just one. No ultrawide, no macro, no nothing extra. At this price point, even budget Android phones ship with three cameras. Apple made a deliberate choice here and buyers should understand what they are signing up for before clicking add to cart. The design quirks pile up fast. No MagSafe (just standard slow wireless charging), no Dynamic Island, a 60Hz display, and a notch that looks lifted straight from an iPhone 14. The phone also arrived eSIM only, which tripped me up during setup if your carrier or workflow is not ready for that. Cosmetically, the renewed unit was clean and showed no real wear, so no complaints there. The Amazon Renewed program handled the process fine. Ultimately I returned it. Not because it is a bad phone, but because the gap between what this costs and what you actually get compared to a used iPhone 16 is just not wide enough to justify the trade-offs. Do yourself a favor and spend a little more for the real thing, or go further down market intentionally.

review_title: Renewed Premium sold and shipped by Amazon is the way to go
review_comment: Lots of mixed reviews made me initially quite hesitant to make this purchase. But I went with Renewed Premium sold and shipped by Amazon—the device arrived in mint condition, unlocked, battery life >90%, and in Amazon’s Renewed Premium packaging which provided protection during shipping. The device also came with an original Apple charging cable in mint condition and a block adapter (not Apple) which both functioned as intended. I had no issues whatsoever. I did a significant amount of research into other options for used iPhone purchases, and I decided this was the best deal because of Amazon’s generous return policy (in the event the device had issues/damage, arrived locked to a carrier, etc) and warranty for Renewed Premium devices. My recommendation is to preferentially purchase a Renewed Premium device direct from Amazon, or if it’s another seller, then be sure to check out their reviews, policies, and info by clicking on the seller’s name. Screen quality was flawless. Zero overheating. Durable enough device, but, as with all iPhones, it is best protected in a reasonably sturdy case with drop protection and a screen protector + camera lens protector. Worth the money when you consider device repair if it is dropped/broken. Appearance is good and the Midnight color is an attractive color. Touch sensitivity was same/similar to a new device.

review_title: Great new-to-me iPhone for an affordable price for basic user!
review_comment: Although my iPhone 6S Plus still works just as well as when I first bought it, it cannot connect to Airtag 2nd generation in the Find My app, so I wanted to get an updated iPhone to use modern Airtags (2nd gen), the Find My app, and the Apple Podcasts app, which has a fantasic auto-generated transcripts feature. I originally got a Renewed/Refurbished iPhone 12, but the battery life was disappointing when compared to iPhone 6S Plus. I paid a few bucks more and upgraded to the iPhone 13 Renewed Premium. It was really worth it! A renewed premium/refurbished iPhone 13 has everything you need for a modern smartphone in 2026: 1. One-year warranty/return period with Amazon. It came with a checklist and a list of all the refurbished/replacements done to the device in the Service History in the About screen on the iPhone. I got 100% battery life since the battery and logic board were replaced. 2. It can run iOS 26, which has a lot of cool, quality-of-life features compared to my iPhone 6S Plus: MagSafe wireless charging, StandBy mode to turn it into a desk calendar/clock screen when horizontal and charging with MagSafe, Category grouping in Mail, Face ID unlock is quick and easy to set up and is blazing fast unlocking the iPhone. 3. The 6.1-inch screen and power button did have hairline scratches, but they disappear with a screen protector and a case, so I don't mind. The display still looks great for 60 Hz! I do not play games on my smartphones, so I don't care about it. The only negatives: 1. iPhone 13 is heavier and thicker than the iPhone 12. 2. I don't think the camera focus of either back lens is as sharp as the iPhone 6S Plus. It takes a long time to focus, especially for close-up shots, and boke is not reliable. I am hoping to keep it for another 5 years, as I trust the quality of Apple and its refurbishment partners.

review_title: My Experience With WirelessSource and The Reputation MD
review_comment: The product arrived damaged and not in the advertised 'excellent' condition. There were many dents along the bottom, and the battery health was 71% instead of the advertised 80%. There may be a message under this review stating that 'the fulfillment issues associated with this order were not due to the seller.' If such a message is present, it is incorrect. The problems were not due to the shipping company or Amazon, they were entirely due to the actions of the seller, Wireless Source, and the review management company they contracted, The Reputation MD. I bought a 256GB Apple iPhone 13 from WirelessSource, also known as Magnakom. This review will detail my experience with this seller. To remain objective, I will describe exactly what happened. When the iPhone arrived, I immediately noticed several bumps and dents on its bottom edge. While concerning, I was willing to overlook it so long as the battery health was above 80%. The iPhone was stated to be in excellent condition on its Amazon listing, and, among other things, the battery health was 71% instead of 80%, meaning the iPhone was not in excellent condition. I figured that WirelessSource would rather keep some of the money than refund me all of it, so I sent a message offering to keep the phone if they would refund me the cost of a new battery. WirelessSource replied by sending a generic message offering a 5% refund if I were to keep the phone, and asked for photos of the problem despite me having already sent them. I let them know I had already sent them, and they sent me a variation of the same message, again asking for pictures. Seeing this and doing additional research on WirelessSource, I made a complaint through the Better Business Bureau. WirelessSource then asked for the IMEI of the device, which I provided. They then claimed it wasn't the same as the IMEI of the phone they shipped. When I pushed back and opted to return the phone instead, they asked for a photo of the packaging, and when I provided it, they conceded that it was the phone they sent, and provided me a shipping label to return it. It was around this time that I began receiving calls and emails from a Todd Lewis of The Reputation MD, a company that regulates and 'cleans up' online reviews for businesses. I ignored these, because I thought speaking to a review management company was abnormal. Returning things at Target, Walmart, eBay, or Amazon itself never required me to do that. Also during this time, WirelessSource sent me a message claiming my device was iCloud locked: i.e. I didn't wipe the iPhone before returning it. I did wipe the iPhone, and after a few back-and-forth messages and photos, (including one where they claimed the IMEI didn't match the order even though we previously confirmed it did,) I recorded a video of me going to my Apple account and FindMyiPhone and demonstrating that I had wiped the phone and it was no longer on my account. After that video, they confirmed the account removal. While this was happening, I filed an A-z Refund claim with Amazon. I didn't have a whole lot of faith that I would be refunded at this point. While the claim was active, Todd Lewis of The Reputation MD sent me a 'refund contract.' This contract was meant to ensure I returned the iPhone (even though at that point they had already received it back,) and it was also meant to prevent me from defaming the company, although I suspected they would try and leverage the contract to prevent me from leaving a negative review. I am not making a concrete claim, though, it was just a suspicion I had. Like before, no other refund I've done has made me do this, and I ignored the contract despite their daily emails. Eventually, Amazon themselves refunded me, and I chose to let the Better Business Bureau complaint go. I continued to ignore their emails, since attempting to get a refund from them on top of Amazon's would be fraud, and eventually they stopped. I wanted to leave this review to recount my experience with WirelessSource/Magnakom as well as Todd Lewis and The Reputation MD. I've tried to be objective so you can draw your own conclusions. I have provided a compilation of the messages between us, although it may take some zooming to see them all. I hope you find this review helpful, and I hope WirelessSource learns to do better.

review_title: My Experience With WirelessSource and The Reputation MD
review_comment: The product arrived damaged and not in the advertised 'excellent' condition. There were many dents along the bottom, and the battery health was 71% instead of the advertised 80%. There may be a message under this review stating that 'the fulfillment issues associated with this order were not due to the seller.' If such a message is present, it is incorrect. The problems were not due to the shipping company or Amazon, they were entirely due to the actions of the seller, Wireless Source, and the review management company they contracted, The Reputation MD. I bought a 256GB Apple iPhone 13 from WirelessSource, also known as Magnakom. This review will detail my experience with this seller. To remain objective, I will describe exactly what happened. When the iPhone arrived, I immediately noticed several bumps and dents on its bottom edge. While concerning, I was willing to overlook it so long as the battery health was above 80%. The iPhone was stated to be in excellent condition on its Amazon listing, and, among other things, the battery health was 71% instead of 80%, meaning the iPhone was not in excellent condition. I figured that WirelessSource would rather keep some of the money than refund me all of it, so I sent a message offering to keep the phone if they would refund me the cost of a new battery. WirelessSource replied by sending a generic message offering a 5% refund if I were to keep the phone, and asked for photos of the problem despite me having already sent them. I let them know I had already sent them, and they sent me a variation of the same message, again asking for pictures. Seeing this and doing additional research on WirelessSource, I made a complaint through the Better Business Bureau. WirelessSource then asked for the IMEI of the device, which I provided. They then claimed it wasn't the same as the IMEI of the phone they shipped. When I pushed back and opted to return the phone instead, they asked for a photo of the packaging, and when I provided it, they conceded that it was the phone they sent, and provided me a shipping label to return it. It was around this time that I began receiving calls and emails from a Todd Lewis of The Reputation MD, a company that regulates and 'cleans up' online reviews for businesses. I ignored these, because I thought speaking to a review management company was abnormal. Returning things at Target, Walmart, eBay, or Amazon itself never required me to do that. Also during this time, WirelessSource sent me a message claiming my device was iCloud locked: i.e. I didn't wipe the iPhone before returning it. I did wipe the iPhone, and after a few back-and-forth messages and photos, (including one where they claimed the IMEI didn't match the order even though we previously confirmed it did,) I recorded a video of me going to my Apple account and FindMyiPhone and demonstrating that I had wiped the phone and it was no longer on my account. After that video, they confirmed the account removal. While this was happening, I filed an A-z Refund claim with Amazon. I didn't have a whole lot of faith that I would be refunded at this point. While the claim was active, Todd Lewis of The Reputation MD sent me a 'refund contract.' This contract was meant to ensure I returned the iPhone (even though at that point they had already received it back,) and it was also meant to prevent me from defaming the company, although I suspected they would try and leverage the contract to prevent me from leaving a negative review. I am not making a concrete claim, though, it was just a suspicion I had. Like before, no other refund I've done has made me do this, and I ignored the contract despite their daily emails. Eventually, Amazon themselves refunded me, and I chose to let the Better Business Bureau complaint go. I continued to ignore their emails, since attempting to get a refund from them on top of Amazon's would be fraud, and eventually they stopped. I wanted to leave this review to recount my experience with WirelessSource/Magnakom as well as Todd Lewis and The Reputation MD. I've tried to be objective so you can draw your own conclusions. I have provided a compilation of the messages between us, although it may take some zooming to see them all. I hope you find this review helpful, and I hope WirelessSource learns to do better.

I originally got a Renewed/Refurbished iPhone 12, but the battery life was disappointing when compared to iPhone 6S Plus. I paid a few bucks more and upgraded to the iPhone 13 Renewed Premium. It was really worth it! A renewed premium/refurbished iPhone 13 has everything you need for a modern smartphone in 2026: 1. One-year warranty/return period with Amazon. It came with a checklist and a list of all the refurbished/replacements done to the device in the Service History in the About screen on the iPhone. I got 100% battery life since the battery and logic board were replaced. 2. It can run iOS 26, which has a lot of cool, quality-of-life features compared to my iPhone 6S Plus: MagSafe wireless charging, StandBy mode to turn it into a desk calendar/clock screen when horizontal and charging with MagSafe, Category grouping in Mail, Face ID unlock is quick and easy to set up and is blazing fast unlocking the iPhone. 3. The 6.1-inch screen and power button did have hairline scratches, but they disappear with a screen protector and a case, so I don't mind. The display still looks great for 60 Hz! I do not play games on my smartphones, so I don't care about it. The only negatives: 1. iPhone 13 is heavier and thicker than the iPhone 12. 2. I don't think the camera focus of either back lens is as sharp as the iPhone 6S Plus. It takes a long time to focus, especially for close-up shots, and boke is not reliable. I am hoping to keep it for another 5 years, as I trust the quality of Apple and its refurbishment partners.

review_comment: I recently ordered an iPhone 13 for my son to use for school. I was a little hesitant about ordering a refurbished phone from Amazon, but the price was too good to pass up. The phone itself seems to work well so far, and considering the price, I’m still satisfied overall. However, describing the cosmetic condition as “excellent” feels misleading. I would consider the phone I received to be closer to “good” condition. If cosmetic appearance is important to you, I’d keep that in mind before purchasing.

review_title: My Experience With WirelessSource and The Reputation MD
review_comment: The product arrived damaged and not in the advertised 'excellent' condition. There were many dents along the bottom, and the battery health was 71% instead of the advertised 80%. There may be a message under this review stating that 'the fulfillment issues associated with this order were not due to the seller.' If such a message is present, it is incorrect. The problems were not due to the shipping company or Amazon, they were entirely due to the actions of the seller, Wireless Source, and the review management company they contracted, The Reputation MD. I bought a 256GB Apple iPhone 13 from WirelessSource, also known as Magnakom. This review will detail my experience with this seller. To remain objective, I will describe exactly what happened. When the iPhone arrived, I immediately noticed several bumps and dents on its bottom edge. While concerning, I was willing to overlook it so long as the battery health was above 80%. The iPhone was stated to be in excellent condition on its Amazon listing, and, among other things, the battery health was 71% instead of 80%, meaning the iPhone was not in excellent condition. I figured that WirelessSource would rather keep some of the money than refund me all of it, so I sent a message offering to keep the phone if they would refund me the cost of a new battery. WirelessSource replied by sending a generic message offering a 5% refund if I were to keep the phone, and asked for photos of the problem despite me having already sent them. I let them know I had already sent them, and they sent me a variation of the same message, again asking for pictures. Seeing this and doing additional research on WirelessSource, I made a complaint through the Better Business Bureau. WirelessSource then asked for the IMEI of the device, which I provided. They then claimed it wasn't the same as the IMEI of the phone they shipped. When I pushed back and opted to return the phone instead, they asked for a photo of the packaging, and when I provided it, they conceded that it was the phone they sent, and provided me a shipping label to return it. It was around this time that I began receiving calls and emails from a Todd Lewis of The Reputation MD, a company that regulates and 'cleans up' online reviews for businesses. I ignored these, because I thought speaking to a review management company was abnormal. Returning things at Target, Walmart, eBay, or Amazon itself never required me to do that. Also during this time, WirelessSource sent me a message claiming my device was iCloud locked: i.e. I didn't wipe the iPhone before returning it. I did wipe the iPhone, and after a few back-and-forth messages and photos, (including one where they claimed the IMEI didn't match the order even though we previously confirmed it did,) I recorded a video of me going to my Apple account and FindMyiPhone and demonstrating that I had wiped the phone and it was no longer on my account. After that video, they confirmed the account removal. While this was happening, I filed an A-z Refund claim with Amazon. I didn't have a whole lot of faith that I would be refunded at this point. While the claim was active, Todd Lewis of The Reputation MD sent me a 'refund contract.' This contract was meant to ensure I returned the iPhone (even though at that point they had already received it back,) and it was also meant to prevent me from defaming the company, although I suspected they would try and leverage the contract to prevent me from leaving a negative review. I am not making a concrete claim, though, it was just a suspicion I had. Like before, no other refund I've done has made me do this, and I ignored the contract despite their daily emails. Eventually, Amazon themselves refunded me, and I chose to let the Better Business Bureau complaint go. I continued to ignore their emails, since attempting to get a refund from them on top of Amazon's would be fraud, and eventually they stopped. I wanted to leave this review to recount my experience with WirelessSource/Magnakom as well as Todd Lewis and The Reputation MD. I've tried to be objective so you can draw your own conclusions. I have provided a compilation of the messages between us, although it may take some zooming to see them all. I hope you find this review helpful, and I hope WirelessSource learns to do better.

review_title: iPhone 13 mini is everything I ever wanted.iPhone 13 mini is everything I ever wanted.
review_comment: I’m writing this review with a few caveats I will get to. First of all, the iPhone 13 mini is truly the best iPhone for people who want a phone that feels like a phone and not like they are carrying around a tablet. I have been using the iPhone 16 Pro since it came out and had no idea what I was missing in this older model until I was talking to a friend about his. He told me it was the best phone ever made and he would not get rid of his until he couldn’t get replacement parts or unless they made a new updated mini, which it sounds like they have no plans to do (a shame). I was telling him that I have been traveling with work and when I’m pulling a bag, I need to be able to work my phone well with one hand. The 16 Pro is not good for this. I don’t like cases, I don’t want to use a pop socket - I just want a pretty sleek unencumbered iPhone. So I was on a mission and it’s not an easy one when you’re picky about the condition and the phone can only be found in the used/renewed/refurbished channels. I had hesitations about buying from Amazon resale because of other items I’ve gotten from them that didn’t seem like they were inspected. I took a risk. I purchased the starlight 256gb from Amazon (not a marketplace seller). It was still a pretty penny considering the age of the mini, but the minis hold their value due to the cult following they have. I received it and it was absolutely perfect - didn’t look like it had ever been used, though the battery capacity was 85%…which was okay but nothing wonderful. In the meantime, I decided I would prefer the 512gb since I plan to keep this a long time, so I decided to order one, also from Amazon resale, since the 256 was in such pristine condition and I knew I had 90 days to decide regardless. The 512gb through Amazon was a crazy price…marked as excellent but over $550 with taxes (I had paid $330 for the 256gb). Cut to a day later, I see that a seller has the 512 starlight marked as excellent and it was $385. I reached out to them and asked them about the battery health and they were wonderful - got back to me really quickly and said 99%. So I thought, well, for $385 vs $550, I’ll cancel the Amazon order and order this one. Unfortunately it was too late to cancel the Amazon one - it had already shipped - so my intention was to just send it straight back as soon as it was delivered. The one from the actual cellphone reseller got here quickly and for the price, was represented well - it did have 2 corners with blemishes that look like they’re from a drop, but they weren’t terrible but having seen the pristine 256gb version from Amazon, I was being overly picky. The battery was 100%, as they had told me, which was great, but what I noticed was the screen had been replaced. I’m okay with screen replacements - any phone from 2021 has probably had one, as well as any battery that shows 100% on a phone from 2021 is a replaced battery. These are not bad things. What I do know from having a screen replaced years ago through one of the shops that uses an aftermarket part is the screens are not as flat as apple’s genuine screen if you get a replacement from them. It almost has waves in it, especially along the edges. They look fine if you aren’t picky to the degree I am, or looking at the phone from an angle, but I’ve found they are not always reliable screens with regard to the responsiveness. As soon as I saw this, I packed it back up and set up a return through the seller and took it straight to the UPS store. Cut to my next Amazon delivery, the 512gb model that I had been unable to cancel arrives. Since the one from the reseller didn’t work out for me, I said, well, let’s check this out because if it’s perfect, then I guess it’s worth the $550 spent. Open it up and WOW! The body of it is just like the 256 I had gotten. Pristine - not a drop ding or scratch in sight. Perfect screen…remarkable…but I wanted to check the battery. When I got it up and running, I checked the battery capacity and it was at 100%. Under the battery details it even lists it as a Genuine battery, so it was “renewed” with Apple OEM. I could not be more thrilled even though it cost way more than a phone from 2021 should. But I’m keeping it for the long haul so it’s worth it knowing I don’t have a battery replacement in the near future. I’ve got the 90 days to see how it functions but I feel pretty good about this one. TL;DR - the iPhone mini is a phone you will be addicted to after use. It’s so functional and what a “phone” should be. Do not hesitate to order one shipped from and sold by Amazon.com. I can confirm they have fantastic quality control when it comes to their phones. If you pick a reseller other than Amazon, just make sure you get the 90 day return and that there aren’t “restocking” fees buried in their policies.

review_title: Pleasantly surprised. Excellent condition, no scratches or dings, passed two diagnostics..
review_comment: I was on a waiting list for a 'Renewed Premium'. Seemed to be a long waiting list. I finally gave up and went with a 'Renewed' advertised in excellent condition. Given Amazon's generous return policy, returning it would have been painless if there had been issues. I probably wouldn't have tried this with an online retailer other than Amazon and Apple. The supplier was TECHMINT, Amazon the purchase portal. There seems to be a number of 'Amazon-qualified suppliers' involved. To know who you're buying from, the 'ships from/sold by' info. is on the right side of the product page. There may also be differences in packaging and accessories. Best to read through the advertising to know exactly what you're buying. Or contact the supplier before purchasing. Given that Amazon backs these purchases, not a concern. It arrived without scratches, dings, or apparent wear. Looks like new. That said, those buying a 'Renewed' phone should expect varying degrees of condition within the parameters of Amazon's advertising. I'd suggest buying a 'Renewed Premium' for your best chance of a like-new phone. I probably got lucky with a 'Renewed'. It shipped in a *very* well designed and protective box designed for phones. Not much larger than the boxes Apple packages iPhones in and similarly sturdy. Well suited for protecting the phone during shipping. If you plan on shipping your phone or storing a back-up, I'd suggest keeping it. The box has spacers to accommodate different sizes. Kudos to the packaging engineers. Well done. It was delivered with 100% battery health which almost certainly means that the phone was opened up and the battery replaced. The likelihood of a 'renewed' 13 Mini arriving with battery health at 100% is slim to none. I assume that they did this because the phone was traded in with < 80% battery health. Amazon advertising states that the phone will arrive with battery health of ≥ 80%. Notably, the battery was recognized by iOS as 'genuine' (thanks TECHMINT). Batteries that are not can lead to various issues, most importantly, safety issues. Look up "how to check if an iPhone battery is genuine". If it isn't, I'd suggest returning it to the supplier. Side note about iPhone battery replacement: If/when you have an iPhone battery replaced, I'd highly recommend scheduling it through Apple. Apple often contracts with third parties to do this in addition to Apple stores. When third parties sign up for this, they're held to a high standard and you're guaranteed to receive a 'genuine' battery. More importantly, if there's a problem you'll have the full weight of Apple behind you to resolve any issues. I'd also suggest reaching out to the supplier before purchase and asking what the battery health will be. In my experience with the iPhone 12 Mini, once you drop into the high 80% range, battery life becomes more noticeable. Note that Apple recommends replacing an iPhone battery when it reaches 80% battery health. I ran two diagnostics to check functions. In both cases, no issues. One of the diagnostics is built into iOS. You'll need iOS 17 or later and not a beta release. Search for 'built in iPhone diagnostic' for instructions. There's another which makes doing this quite a bit easier. From the Apple app store search for 'Phone Doctor Plus'. It's not a diagnostic as much as it's a function check but good for making sure everything works. There's a free and paid version. There are others but these are the only two I've tried. The advertising stated that an MFi certified charging/data cable ships with the phone. Mine shipped with a 3ft braided USB C to Lightning charging cable. No branding or print on the cable, no included documentation, no packaging. It appears similar to what you'll sometimes see without packaging and hanging from peg racks in convenience stores. I have no reason to believe that the provided cable isn't MFi certified and from a reliable manufacturer but without more information, best to use an Apple product or something from an established aftermarket supplier such as Belkin or Anker. Look for 'MFi certified' especially if you want fast charging capability. There are reasons USB C cables can be pricey, especially those designed for high power delivery. Mine shipped without a charger. I'd say the same about a charger as I did about the cable - MFi certified and from a reputable manufacturer - Apple, Belkin, Anker, etc. For the 13 Mini, Apple recommends a minimum of a 20 watt charger for optimal/fast charging . Apple's is about 20 dollars. It's also what Apple recommends for powering *the original* MagSafe accessory. The updated version of the MagSafe charger supports faster charging and according to Apple, a minimum of a 30 watt charger for optimal performance. Some suppliers advertise that a sim card removal tool is included. Mine didn't. If yours shipped with a sim card (mine did not), I'd suggest reading through the pros and cons of SIM vs eSIM. If eSIM meets your needs, I'd recommend removing the SIM and switching to eSIM. Switching to eSIM can be done in your phone's settings. No expertise or hardware required. Although unlikely if buying from an 'Amazon-qualified supplier' (I assume), SIM cards can be compromised. If you need a SIM card, best to get one from your carrier instead of a mystery SIM. The Apple leather case has been my go-to for the last 2-3 iPhones. Very well designed, doesn't add significant bulk, comfortable to grip, no sharp edges and it slips into and out of a pocket easily. The drop protection has proven to be excellent. Great case for all but extreme circumstances. They're relatively pricey so If you're looking to save, there are often Amazon customer returns available. eBay is another good source. The iPhone 12 mini and 13 mini cases are not interchangeable. I tried. The camera lens housings are different. The 12 mini case will not fit the 13 mini. The 13 mini case will fit the 12 mini but there will be a gap on the right side of the lens housing. Not to overstate it but If you're considering both the 12 mini and 13 mini, battery life may be problematic for heavy users. If you have a full size phone with a larger battery at ≥ 90% battery health (guesstimate) and often find yourself scrambling to find a charger, the Mini may not be for you. If you're on the move a lot without convenient charging options, a small power bank (≤ 5000mAh) will bring some peace of mind and a lot of convenience. Great when traveling. Definitely stick with time tested manufacturers. Anker and Belkin sell a wide variety. Note that the TSA only allows powerbanks in carry-ons. Apple discontinued it's iPhone power banks (Magsafe Battery Pack). As of this writing, you can still find them new from third party sources such as Walmart and eBay. Never buy used. There are confirmed and very convincing counterfeits out there so I'd be cautious about which supplier you choose. Look up "how to check if an Apple Magsafe Battery Pack is counterfeit". *Update* Apple reintroduced it's magsafe battery pack now called the iPhone Air MagSafe Battery. It was designed specifically for the iPhone Air and reportedly works with other iPhones - sort of. Not recommended. Fit issues. If you're looking at both the 12 and 13 Minis, the 13 Mini uses an A15 processor which is somewhat more energy efficient and slightly faster. It also has a ~10% larger battery. There are quite a few other differences including an upgraded camera. In day to day use, I found the differences to be negligible. I suspect that most people wouldn't be able to tell the difference without knowing what to look for. Definitely worth reading comparison reviews. Some of the updates will be important for some, less so for others. Search for "iPhone 13 mini vs iPhone 12 mini". If you read only one, Laptopmag.com published a well grounded, real-world comparison, no hype. Long term, the 13 Mini will receive system/feature updates from Apple for about a year longer. This may be the most value added difference. Generally speaking, Apple devices continue to receive security updates beyond the point that they are no longer supported with system/feature updates. Current estimates seem to be late 2027 for system/feature updates and 2030/2031 for security updates. When the security updates stop, best to replace the phone. If Apple's AI (Apple Intelligence) is a feature you want, it isn't supported in the Mini's. You can still use cloud based AI services but without the privacy and security features Apple bakes into it's AI. You'll need a minimum of an iPhone 15 Pro or Pro Max to use Apple's AI. Happy customer. I'm fully committed to the Mini form factor/dimensions. I carry it all day in a front or back pocket and barely know it's there. Having a phone with more screen, battery and features is nice but after the novelty wears off, having a phone that disappears into a pocket is more important for some of us. Sadly, not enough of us for Apple to justify continued production. When I need to replace it, perhaps Mini's will be back in the menu from Apple. Hope so.

review_comment: The phone I received was by all estimations brand new. Not a mark on it and fully charged. Even its keyboard is not a full Standard Keyboard, like it is with Windows & any Google machine. Android is Google, that's why I say it that way. No getting around it. Just keeping it short & to the point. Apple's iPhone keyboard takes extreme amount of effort to use because it is not the Standard keyboard of every other operating system. There's no such thing as the simple pinch & zoom on it. That particular luxury seems to be found only within the Camera & Picture sections. You'd think it'd at least be within the iBook section but it's not. On most everything Windows or Google, every app is not just touch & activate, but also affords the luxury of pinch & zoom as well as easy swipe & easy app close & dismiss. Can't say that about the Apple iPhone. And for some unknown reason its WiFi also keeps turning itself on. I can't seem to keep it off no matter how often I manually turn it off. For Apple being so USER-FRIENDLY, I cannot at all say that it is. In fact, IT IS ANYTHING BUT USER-FRIENDLY. If the Apple World was so user-friendly, then it would be a very simple and easy transition from the Windows or Google platform to Apple. And I can honestly say it is Not at all simple or easy. I was so hoping it would be as simple & easy as my Windows machine & Android phone, but sadly, it's actually quite maddening. If you enjoy Kindle reads, you'll need to install the app for it. But I can also tell you, Apple's iBook seriously pales in comparison to Kindle. Ironically, the Google Search Engine is installed on Apple's iPhone but Kindle is not. I avoid Google anything & everything as much as can be done. But for Apple to deny Amazon's Kindle Apple on its phones, seems almost a crime. I have yet to install the Kindle reading app or to test out the camera on the iPhone. When I do I'll update my review. But currently I can't say it's anything to brag about. And I most certainly did not expect to see Google's Search Engine/Web Browser on it. Size wise, it's the exact same size as my Sony Xperia Z3v. It still functions quite well. Not perfect, but well enough for me since I have it locked to call, text, Kindle reads & camera. I can easily read, pinch & zoom & highlight my Kindle reads, pictures & text messages on it. Can only do that with pictures on the iPhone. So for it being so great, I actually find it quite limiting. Not because it's an iPhone, but because the Apple creators decided to create a platform that is quite complex and extremely arduous to use. Apple created its own "language" that must be learned in order to navigate the complexities of its Eco-system. Even now, trying to login to the Apple App Store, no keyboard appears so I can actually install Apps necessary for my personal use. Yet you're required to sign in to it. How can you sign into the App Store when NO KEYBOARD APPEARS TO LET YOU?! So, even if I did not want to use the phone feature, but instead use it as a computer tablet, I cannot because it won't let me login to the App Store. ... Like I said, to anyone new to the Apple world, it's quite a infuriatingly maddening conundrum. If Apple wants to gain new customers and retain them, then Apple needs to change how it operates. And if Apple is supposed to be the safest of all online platforms, then it should not sport Google's web browser. The phone I received was/is like brand new. Operating it though, takes considerable patients as it is quite the learning curve. It should not be so difficult to transition from Windows, Android or Google to Apple. They all made sense to everybody from the moment they came out because they were in simple English and easily understood and simple to navigate because of it. Apple on the other hand, not by a long shot. Even Apple's touchscreen capabilities sorely lacks in comparison. And that's sad. You'd think their touchscreen capabilities would be at least on-par with Windows, Google & Android but it is not. You'd think Apple's touchscreen capabilities might even be better than Windows, Android & Google, but no. Thus far I can find nothing to brag about regarding Apple anything. I was so hoping to find something better about Apple. Instead, I'm greatly disappointed and left seriously frustrated. The iPhone itself came fully charged and appears in brand new condition. It also came with an original Apple Charger. I give the seller a stellar 5 star rating, along with the iPhone I received. I give Apple itself a mediocre 3, even 2 star rating. So to anyone new to the Apple world, maybe an iPad would be easier to use. I started with a phone since I need both a new phone & a new computer and figured Apple would be a serious upgrade to Windows and for sure compared to Google's Android. ... Apple is not at all user-friendly to a first time user. Only Windows, Google & Android can actually claim user-friendly bragging rights, from day one for any first time user. It's very nearly like you gotta go to MIT to learn it. And that's just not right. Will update as I learn how to navigate Apple's world & extremely clunky Eco-system. 1st Time Apple iPhone User Assessment. - Phone - good. - can't give it high marks due to Apple itself. Apple - not worth all the money & certainly nothing to brag about.

review_title: Renewed Premium sold and shipped by Amazon is the way to go
review_comment: Lots of mixed reviews made me initially quite hesitant to make this purchase. But I went with Renewed Premium sold and shipped by Amazon—the device arrived in mint condition, unlocked, battery life >90%, and in Amazon’s Renewed Premium packaging which provided protection during shipping. Durable enough device, but, as with all iPhones, it is best protected in a reasonably sturdy case with drop protection and a screen protector + camera lens protector. Worth the money when you consider device repair if it is dropped/broken. Appearance is good and the Midnight color is an attractive color. Touch sensitivity was same/similar to a new device.

review_title: Great new-to-me iPhone for an affordable price for basic user!
review_comment: Although my iPhone 6S Plus still works just as well as when I first bought it, it cannot connect to Airtag 2nd generation in the Find My app, so I wanted to get an updated iPhone to use modern Airtags (2nd gen), the Find My app, and the Apple Podcasts app, which has a fantasic auto-generated transcripts feature. I originally got a Renewed/Refurbished iPhone 12, but the battery life was disappointing when compared to iPhone 6S Plus. I paid a few bucks more and upgraded to the iPhone 13 Renewed Premium. It was really worth it! A renewed premium/refurbished iPhone 13 has everything you need for a modern smartphone in 2026: 1. One-year warranty/return period with Amazon. It came with a checklist and a list of all the refurbished/replacements done to the device in the Service History in the About screen on the iPhone. I got 100% battery life since the battery and logic board were replaced. 2. It can run iOS 26, which has a lot of cool, quality-of-life features compared to my iPhone 6S Plus: MagSafe wireless charging, StandBy mode to turn it into a desk calendar/clock screen when horizontal and charging with MagSafe, Category grouping in Mail, Face ID unlock is quick and easy to set up and is blazing fast unlocking the iPhone. 3. The 6.1-inch screen and power button did have hairline scratches, but they disappear with a screen protector and a case, so I don't mind. The display still looks great for 60 Hz! I do not play games on my smartphones, so I don't care about it. The only negatives: 1. iPhone 13 is heavier and thicker than the iPhone 12. 2. I don't think the camera focus of either back lens is as sharp as the iPhone 6S Plus. It takes a long time to focus, especially for close-up shots, and boke is not reliable. I am hoping to keep it for another 5 years, as I trust the quality of Apple and its refurbishment partners.

review_title: My Experience With WirelessSource and The Reputation MD
review_comment: The product arrived damaged and not in the advertised 'excellent' condition. There were many dents along the bottom, and the battery health was 71% instead of the advertised 80%. There may be a message under this review stating that 'the fulfillment issues associated with this order were not due to the seller.' If such a message is present, it is incorrect. The problems were not due to the shipping company or Amazon, they were entirely due to the actions of the seller, Wireless Source, and the review management company they contracted, The Reputation MD. I bought a 256GB Apple iPhone 13 from WirelessSource, also known as Magnakom. This review will detail my experience with this seller. To remain objective, I will describe exactly what happened. When the iPhone arrived, I immediately noticed several bumps and dents on its bottom edge. While concerning, I was willing to overlook it so long as the battery health was above 80%. The iPhone was stated to be in excellent condition on its Amazon listing, and, among other things, the battery health was 71% instead of 80%, meaning the iPhone was not in excellent condition. I figured that WirelessSource would rather keep some of the money than refund me all of it, so I sent a message offering to keep the phone if they would refund me the cost of a new battery. WirelessSource replied by sending a generic message offering a 5% refund if I were to keep the phone, and asked for photos of the problem despite me having already sent them. I let them know I had already sent them, and they sent me a variation of the same message, again asking for pictures. Seeing this and doing additional research on WirelessSource, I made a complaint through the Better Business Bureau. WirelessSource then asked for the IMEI of the device, which I provided. They then claimed it wasn't the same as the IMEI of the phone they shipped. When I pushed back and opted to return the phone instead, they asked for a photo of the packaging, and when I provided it, they conceded that it was the phone they sent, and provided me a shipping label to return it. It was around this time that I began receiving calls and emails from a Todd Lewis of The Reputation MD, a company that regulates and 'cleans up' online reviews for businesses. I ignored these, because I thought speaking to a review management company was abnormal. Returning things at Target, Walmart, eBay, or Amazon itself never required me to do that. Also during this time, WirelessSource sent me a message claiming my device was iCloud locked: i.e. I didn't wipe the iPhone before returning it. I did wipe the iPhone, and after a few back-and-forth messages and photos, (including one where they claimed the IMEI didn't match the order even though we previously confirmed it did,) I recorded a video of me going to my Apple account and FindMyiPhone and demonstrating that I had wiped the phone and it was no longer on my account. After that video, they confirmed the account removal. While this was happening, I filed an A-z Refund claim with Amazon. I didn't have a whole lot of faith that I would be refunded at this point. While the claim was active, Todd Lewis of The Reputation MD sent me a 'refund contract.' This contract was meant to ensure I returned the iPhone (even though at that point they had already received it back,) and it was also meant to prevent me from defaming the company, although I suspected they would try and leverage the contract to prevent me from leaving a negative review. I am not making a concrete claim, though, it was just a suspicion I had. Like before, no other refund I've done has made me do this, and I ignored the contract despite their daily emails. Eventually, Amazon themselves refunded me, and I chose to let the Better Business Bureau complaint go. I continued to ignore their emails, since attempting to get a refund from them on top of Amazon's would be fraud, and eventually they stopped. I wanted to leave this review to recount my experience with WirelessSource/Magnakom as well as Todd Lewis and The Reputation MD. I've tried to be objective so you can draw your own conclusions. I have provided a compilation of the messages between us, although it may take some zooming to see them all. I hope you find this review helpful, and I hope WirelessSource learns to do better.
